posts.title: Nevada put medical cannabis in its constitution
posts.summary: Nevada voters said yes to Question 9 in 1998 and again in 2000. Here is the section they added, the two-vote rule that made them vote twice, the official counts, and what the text left for lawmakers to build.

slides.alt: The Nevada State Capitol in Carson City, a stone building with a silver dome, seen at the end of a walk lined with trees, lamp posts with Battle Born 150 banners and flagpoles; no people in frame. Slide text: Nevada put medical cannabis in its constitution. The Nevada State Capitol, Carson City. Voters approved Question 9 in 1998 and again in 2000. It became Article 4, section 38.

A crop of the Nevada Legislature's page of the Nevada Constitution: Article 4, section 38, Use of plant of genus Cannabis for medical purposes, subsection 1 and paragraph (a) listing the conditions. Slide text: The text is an order to lawmakers. Section 38 begins: "The legislature shall provide by law for" use by a patient, on a physician's advice, for listed conditions.

A crop of the scanned 1998 Nevada ballot booklet: Question No. 9, Amendment to the Nevada Constitution, and the condensation asking whether to allow the possession and use of a plant of the genus Cannabis for certain illnesses. Slide text: 1998: the question on the ballot. Question 9 asked whether to allow possession and use of cannabis for certain illnesses, on a physician's advice, with parental consent for minors.

A crop of the Nevada Secretary of State's 1998 Official General Election Returns: the Yes and No rows for Question 9 with one column per county, totals 241,510 yes and 170,264 no. Slide text: First vote: 58.7 percent yes. Official 1998 returns: 241,510 yes and 170,264 no. Ten of Nevada's 17 counties voted yes.
slides.credit: Source: NV Sec. of State, 1998 returns

slides.alt: A crop of the Nevada Constitution, Article 19, section 2(4): if a majority approves, the Secretary of State shall publish and resubmit the question at the next succeeding general election, and a second approval makes it part of the Constitution. Slide text: One yes was not enough. For an initiative amendment, Article 19 sends the question back to voters at the next general election. It needs a second majority.

A crop of the Secretary of State's letter in the 2000 Nevada ballot booklet: Ballot Question Number 9 passed at the 1998 General Election and appears for the second and last time on the 2000 General Election Ballot. Slide text: 2000: "the second and last time." The Secretary of State's 2000 ballot booklet said Question 9 passed in 1998 and was back for its final vote.

A crop of the scanned 2000 Nevada ballot booklet: Question No. 9 and its condensation, with 381,947 written by hand beside Yes, checked, and 202,211 beside No. Slide text: Second vote: 65.4 percent yes. Official 2000 results: 381,947 yes and 202,211 no. Only Lincoln and White Pine counties voted no.

A crop of the Nevada Constitution, Article 4, section 38(1)(d) and (e): a registry of patients and their attendants that law enforcement may use to verify a claim and that is otherwise confidential, and authorization of appropriate methods for supply of the plant. Slide text: A registry, and a way to supply. The Legislature must create a confidential registry police can check, and authorize "appropriate methods for supply." The text does not say which.

A crop of the Nevada Constitution, Article 4, section 38(2): the section does not authorize use other than medical or medical use in public, or require reimbursement by an insurer or accommodation at work, with the note that it was approved in 1998 and 2000. Slide text: What section 38 does not do. No non-medical use, no medical use in public, no required insurance payment. Insurance and patient access are on the MJBizCon 2026 program, Thursday, Dec. 3.

A crop of page 3053 of the Statutes of Nevada 2001: Assembly Bill No. 453, Assemblywoman Giunchigliani, Chapter 592, an act exempting the medical use of marijuana from state prosecution in certain circumstances, approved June 14, 2001. Slide text: 2001: the Legislature answered. AB 453 became Chapter 592, approved June 14, 2001; most of it took effect Oct. 1. A companion piece covers 2001 to 2015.

posts.title: Three stripes, four emails
posts.summary: In 2023 a Manhattan jury decided that Thom Browne's four bars did not infringe adidas's three stripes. Months later, four internal emails surfaced in a London lawsuit, and they said the bars could "look like Adidas." The court papers show what happened next, and why the emails never got the case reopened.

slides.alt: A typed court form headed Verdict, with handwritten check marks beside Not Liable for trademark infringement and for trademark dilution, and blank damages lines.
Printed court text quoting an email: as Adidas has such a big presence in the sporting world, it is inevitable that our 4bar in white be read as adidas stripes, especially on accessories.
Printed court text saying a paralegal had carried out a mass edit on documents that hit on the search term adidas, including the four emails, changing their fields to needs further review.
Typewritten court text ending: An inadvertent but understandable mix-up is not the same as negligence, at least not here.

Printed court text: because misconduct under Rule 60(b)(3) does not encompass merely negligent discovery violations, and Thom Browne's failure was no more than negligent, adidas is not entitled to relief.
Printed court text saying likelihood of confusion is an objective standard and the emails reflected executives' opinions, then that adidas's consumer survey did not persuade the jury.
The west front of the U.S. Supreme Court building at dusk, its white columns lit from inside above wide steps.

onScreen: Three stripes, four emails. In January 2023 a jury found Thom Browne not liable for infringing adidas's three stripes. The emails came later.
Four internal emails surfaced in a London case. One said it was "inevitable that our 4bar in white be read as adidas stripes." The New York jury never saw them.
A mass edit kept them out of the case. A paralegal tagged documents that hit on "adidas" as "needs further review," so the privilege search skipped them.
2024: the trial judge called it a mix-up. Judge Rakoff held that negligence could count as misconduct, then found the law firm had not been negligent.
2026: negligent, but not misconduct. The Second Circuit found the firm negligent and held that negligence alone cannot reopen a final judgment.
Confusion is an objective test. The emails were executives' opinions, the court wrote, and adidas's own consumer survey had not persuaded the jury.
Now adidas has asked the Supreme Court. It asks whether a negligent failure to produce documents can be misconduct. Thom Browne's reply was due Dec. 2, 2026.

posts.title: Protection without a storefront: Nevada medical cannabis, 2001 to 2016
posts.summary: Nevada's constitution asked for a way to supply patients. The first law gave them a card and a plant limit, and left supply to the patients. This is the documentary trail from that law to the first dispensaries.

slides.alt: An aerial photo of the Nevada State Capitol in Carson City: a sandstone building with a white cupola and flags, bare spring trees and hills behind; no people in frame. Slide text: The constitution promised a supply. The first dispensary came 15 years later. Nevada's Capitol in Carson City, 2025. Voters put medical cannabis in the constitution in 2000. The state dates its first dispensary to August 2015.

A crop of a Nevada Legislature exhibit reprinting the state constitution, Article 4, section 38, paragraphs (d) and (e): a confidential registry of patients and attendants, and authorization of appropriate methods for supply of the plant to patients. Slide text: The constitution asked lawmakers for a supply. Article 4, section 38 called for a confidential patient registry and "appropriate methods for supply of the plant" to patients.

A crop of Nevada Assembly Bill 453 of 2001, in blue italic type: do not, at any one time, collectively possess, deliver or produce more than one ounce of usable marijuana, three mature marijuana plants and four immature marijuana plants. Slide text: 2001: a card, one ounce, seven plants. AB 453 let a cardholder and caregiver hold, together, one ounce of usable marijuana, three mature plants and four immature plants at any one time.

A crop of Nevada Assembly Bill 453 of 2001, paragraph (f): delivering marijuana for consideration to any person, regardless of whether the recipient lawfully holds a registry identification card. Slide text: Selling it stayed a crime. The same law gave no exemption for delivering marijuana "for consideration" to any person, even another cardholder. Patients could grow it or receive it free.

A crop of Nevada Assembly Bill 453 of 2001, section 30.5: the department shall vigorously pursue federal approval to establish a bank or repository of seeds, and a program to produce and deliver marijuana to people using it under the law. Slide text: The state's own supply plan never arrived. AB 453 told the Agriculture Department to seek federal approval for a seed bank and a state supply program. A 2012 court order said: "This has not been done."

A crop of a scanned, line-numbered Nevada district court order, lines 21 to 26: the law strips anyone possessing marijuana in a place open to the public of the exemption, which necessarily prevents any store front medical marijuana provider. Slide text: A judge said the law blocked any storefront. In February 2012, District Judge Donald Mosley wrote that the law "necessarily prevents any store front medical marijuana provider." Prosecutors appealed.

A crop of Nevada Senate Judiciary Committee minutes: William J. Baker says he is a retired autoworker and disabled American, that without dispensaries he let his license expire, and that he was unable to grow his own and there was no place to buy it. Slide text: "There was no place to buy it." A retired autoworker told senators in March 2013 he let his card lapse. He was disabled, could not grow his own, and Nevada had no dispensaries.

A crop of Nevada Senate Bill 374 of 2013, section 11: dispensary certificates of 40 in a county of 700,000 or more, 10 in a county of 100,000 to 700,000, 2 in a county of 55,000 to 100,000, and 1 in each other county. Slide text: 2013: dispensaries capped by county size. SB 374 set 40 dispensary certificates for the largest county, 10 for the next size, 2 for mid-size counties and 1 for each other county.

A crop of the Nevada medical marijuana program web page timeline: 519 applications in August 2014; 372 provisional certificates on November 3, 2014, 55 of them for dispensaries; first final certifications in March 2015; first dispensary opening in August 2015, in Sparks. Slide text: 2014: 519 applications, 372 provisional certificates. Applications ran for 10 days in August 2014. The Division's own timeline dates the first dispensary opening to August 2015, in Sparks. It names no store.
slides.credit: Source: Nevada DPBH web page, 2017 copy

slides.alt: A Nevada health division presentation slide headed Who is fully operational, as of March 16, 2016: dispensaries 33 percent, 22 of 66; cultivation 38 of 182; production 17 of 118; laboratories 7 of 17; aggregate 84 of 383. Slide text: By March 2016, 22 dispensaries were fully operational. The Division's count for March 16, 2016: 22 of 66 dispensaries "fully operational." That was about 15 years after voters approved the amendment.

posts.title: Nevada borrowed its cannabis regulator from the casino floor
posts.summary: In 2019 Nevada built its Cannabis Compliance Board from the parts of its gaming regulator. The statutes show what was copied, what was changed, and what the Legislature took back in 2023 and 2025.

slides.alt: The Nevada Legislative Building in Carson City on a sunny day: a pale stone building with a silver dome behind trees, a street lamp and a low wall reading Nevada State Assembly; no people in frame. Slide text: Nevada borrowed its cannabis regulator from the casino floor. The Legislative Building, Carson City. AB 533 was heard here in 2019. It made a cannabis board modeled after the Gaming Control Board.

A crop of page 2 of Nevada Assembly Bill 533 (2019): the digest sentence saying section 54 creates the Cannabis Compliance Board of five members appointed by the Governor and generally modeled after the Nevada Gaming Control Board. Slide text: The bill said it plainly. AB 533's digest calls the five-member Cannabis Compliance Board "generally modeled after the Nevada Gaming Control Board." It took over from Taxation on July 1, 2020.

A crop of typed minutes of the Nevada Assembly Committee on Judiciary, May 21, 2019, page 8: the Governor's general counsel says the structure is a lighter one of roughly 45 people as opposed to the 400 in gaming. Slide text: Similar to gaming, but lighter. The Governor's general counsel told lawmakers the cannabis board would have roughly 45 people "as opposed to the 400 in gaming." Those are his estimates.

A crop of page 4 of Nevada Assembly Bill 533: subsection 3 of section 3, saying public confidence and trust can only be maintained by strict regulation of all persons, locations, practices, associations and activities related to cannabis establishments. Slide text: Even the purpose clause echoes gaming law. Like NRS 463.0129, section 3 says "Public confidence and trust can only be maintained by strict regulation of all persons, locations, practices, associations and activities."

A crop of page 14 of Nevada Assembly Bill 533: section 55, the board seats for investigation or law enforcement, a Nevada attorney, the cannabis industry, and a physician, psychologist, counselor or social worker. Slide text: Five seats instead of three. Like the three-member Gaming Control Board, it needs a finance expert and an investigator. It adds a lawyer, a cannabis-industry seat and a health or counseling seat.

posts.title: In Clark County, cannabis regulation can reach the magazine and the consultant
posts.summary: Clark County's licensing packet names cannabis magazines and consultants as support businesses. Here is what the county code, three county ordinances and Nevada's advertising law each say, where they differ, and what the documents do not show.

slides.alt: The sandstone pyramid of the Clark County Government Center in Las Vegas, 2011, seen up close with a band of skylights near its peak, under a deep blue sky, with the red sandstone office wing at its edge; no people in frame. Slide text: In Clark County, cannabis rules can reach the magazine. Clark County Government Center, 2011. County papers list magazines and consultants as support businesses.

A crop of Clark County's support business instructions: any person whose business provides ancillary support to cannabis establishments or the industry must apply for a county business license; such businesses include cannabis-related media outlets (magazines and other publications), cannabis business consulting and medical cannabis patient consulting. Slide text: The county's packet names magazines. The county's support business packet lists "magazines and other publications" and business and patient consultants. The list is open-ended.

A crop of a 2022 Clark County bill, section 8.65.110: item 3, more than fifty percent of the business's total annual revenue within Clark County comes from cannabis products or services, then a list of support services beginning with security services and consulting services. Slide text: The code adds a revenue test. County code defines a support business as one earning over half its Clark County revenue from cannabis work. Consulting is on its list. Media is not named.

A crop of Clark County's support business instructions: once public safety inspections are done and agencies have signed off, the Department schedules a Code Conference with the applicant to review County Code requirements for the cannabis support business. Slide text: Licensing ends in a code conference. After safety inspections and agency sign-offs, the county schedules a code conference to review the county code rules that may affect the support business.

A crop of a 2022 Clark County bill, section 8.65.160, Duties of licensee, with underlined added words extending the duties to holders of an adult-use cannabis support business license. Slide text: Since 2022, support licensees share the duties. An amendment approved December 20, 2022 added support business license holders to the chapter's duties section.

A crop of a 2020 Clark County bill, section 8.65.190, Signs and advertising: an adult-use cannabis establishment shall not use misleading advertising or advertising material that has not been approved by the department, with older state agency wording struck out. Slide text: Establishment ads need the county's approval. County code says a cannabis establishment shall not use advertising material the county department has not approved. The rule is written for the establishment.

A crop of Nevada Revised Statutes 678B.520, paragraph (b): an establishment shall not advertise in any publication or on radio, television or any other medium if 30 percent or more of the audience is reasonably expected to be under 21. Slide text: State law: no ads where 30 percent are under 21. Nevada bars a cannabis establishment from advertising in any publication or medium whose audience is reasonably expected to be 30 percent or more under 21.

A crop of Nevada Revised Statutes 678B.520, subsection 13: local governments may adopt stricter cannabis advertising ordinances on signs and on handbills, pamphlets and cards, excluding an advertisement in a newspaper of general circulation, trade publication or other print media. Slide text: Local limits on handouts stop at print media. Local governments may be stricter than the state on signs and handouts. The handout power excludes ads in newspapers, trade publications and other print media.

A crop of Nevada Revised Statutes 678B.530, subsection 2: a local government shall not regulate the content of an advertisement for the sale of cannabis unless it adopts an ordinance setting forth such regulations. Slide text: Ad content rules need an ordinance. Nevada says a local government may not regulate the content of a cannabis sale ad unless it adopts an ordinance setting out those rules.

The Las Vegas Convention Center facade in 2008: a pale wall with the center's name in large letters, flagpoles, trees and a fenced forecourt under a blue sky; no people close enough to recognize. Slide text: MJBizCon meets on unincorporated county land. The county says the convention center is unincorporated. A Dec. 1 session covers First Amendment issues in cannabis marketing.

onScreen: Where a Hawaiʻi beach ends. In Hawaiʻi the public shore runs up to the highest reach of the winter waves, shown by plants or a line of debris.
1968: the court read three Hawaiian words. Two 1866 royal patents ran "ma ke kai," along the sea. The court held that means the upper reach of the waves, not a tide table.
1973: at Kaimū, the plants won. Where a beach shows a debris line and a vegetation line farther inland, the court presumed the year's highest waves reach the plants.
The shore kept moving. The Corps of Engineers mapped Kaimū's shoreline moving inland from about 1915 to 1972, about 170 feet in 57 years.
1977: new land from lava is public. After the 1955 eruption added land at Kehena, the court held that lava land vests in the people of Hawaiʻi. Shown: 1990 lava at Kalapana.

posts.summary: The 2025 hemp law counts the acid form of THC. Here is what the text says, why most of it waits until December 11, 2026, and what no agency has published yet.

posts.title: Every regulated cannabis plant in Nevada gets a data double
posts.summary: Nevada's licensed cannabis market follows each plant twice: once in the grow room and once in a state tracking system. Here is what the law and the regulations require, what the Cannabis Compliance Board's own documents show, and what the system costs a licensee.

slides.alt: Close view of a Cannabis sativa stem with clusters of small pale green male flowers and serrated leaves, against a blue sky, in the botanical garden of the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Germany; no people, tags or products in frame. Slide text: Every regulated plant in Nevada gets a data double. In Nevada's licensed market, each plant also lives as entries in one state system.

A crop of the Nevada Administrative Code, section 678A.050: batch number means a unique numeric or alphanumeric identifier assigned to a batch by a cannabis establishment when the batch is planted. Slide text: The first ID comes at planting. Nevada defines a batch number as a unique code a licensee assigns to a batch of plants when the batch is planted.

A crop of the Nevada Administrative Code, section 678B.217: a cannabis establishment shall use the seed-to-sale tracking system managed by the Board's independent contractor, connect through its application programming interface, pay its fees, and ensure cannabis is tagged as required. Slide text: One state system, one API, and tags. Licensees must use the tracking system run by the Board's chosen contractor, connect through its API, pay its fees and tag cannabis as required.

A crop of the Nevada Administrative Code, section 678D.020, subsection 10: after receipt, the receiving cannabis establishment shall confirm the products are as described in the transportation manifest and separately document any differences in quantity in the seed-to-sale tracking system. Slide text: A transfer is checked at both ends. The receiving business confirms the load matches the manifest and logs any quantity difference in the tracking system.

A crop of the Nevada Administrative Code, section 678B.214, subsection 8: maintain a seed-to-sale tracking system, reconcile raw material to finished product for each job, and provide quarterly physical inventory counts by persons independent of the manufacturing process, with significant variances reported to the Executive Director. Slide text: Four counts a year, by independent staff. Quarterly physical counts by people outside production are reconciled to the perpetual inventory. Significant variances go to the Executive Director.

A crop of a Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board table, the Entry Error row: used only for data entry mistakes, such as transposed numbers or accidental extra digits; must not be used to correct sales-related errors; check marks for all four license types. Slide text: Fixes need a named reason. The Board's 2025 list of adjustment reasons limits Entry Error to typos, such as transposed numbers. It may not be used to fix sales errors.

A crop of Nevada Legislative Auditor report LA20-05, page 7: auditors compared tax returns of 10 cultivators and 5 dispensaries with tracking data for January to June 2018; data did not agree about 70 percent of the time for wholesale returns, and about 57 and 60 percent for retail and sales tax returns. Slide text: In 2018, the data and tax returns disagreed. State auditors found tracking data did not agree with cultivators' wholesale tax returns about 70 percent of the time, January to June 2018.

A crop of a Nevada Department of Taxation page: the fair market value at wholesale effective October 1, 2026, including small bud 729 dollars a pound, flower 1,037 dollars, trim 150 dollars and pre-roll 1,134 dollars, calculated from cultivator transactions in the seed-to-sale tracking system from June 1 to August 31, 2026. Slide text: The logs now help set a tax value. Taxation set the October 2026 flower value at $1,037 a pound from transactions logged in the state system.

A crop of the Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board Item Catalog FAQ, page 2: the catalog may list Metrc package ID numbers, unique identifiers assigned to each product package and shown on the label, and a certificate of analysis linked to the specific package. Slide text: Shoppers see a slice of the data. The state's public Item Catalog shows package ID numbers and a lab certificate linked to each package, for items sold in the last 180 days.
slides.credit: Source: Nevada CCB, Item Catalog FAQ

slides.alt: A crop of Nevada Revised Statutes 678A.455: a Board agent may issue a hold order only under regulations the Board adopts; the regulations must limit hold orders to products that fail a requirement and are a substantial hazard, require notice, and end the hold within 30 days unless extended after a hearing. Slide text: Still open: the hold-order rules. A 2025 law lets Board agents hold hazardous cannabis; past 30 days needs a Board order. The detailed rules it calls for are only proposed.

onScreen: Paradise in Limbo Hawaii's Cannabis Journey and the Road That Keeps Closing
In 2000, Governor Ben Cayetano signed Act 228 into law. The move made Hawaii the first state in the nation to legalize medical cannabis through its legislature, rather than a ballot initiative.
In 2015, the legislature passed Act 241, creating the Medical Cannabis Dispensary Program. The law created a tightly controlled market: eight dispensary licenses.
Hawaii's dispensaries, in dates. Feb. 1, 2017: First production centers cleared to grow; Aug. 8, 2017: First dispensary cleared to sell; Dec. 23, 2025: 24 retail locations open.
Registered patients peaked at 35,444 in August 2021. By November 2024 the count was 30,035, down more than 15 percent, the Legislature found in 2025.
Speaker Nakamura confirmed that neither HB 1624 nor HB 1625 had enough support to advance. SB 2421, the Senate companion to HB 1625, was heard in committee on February 17, 2026 and did not advance.
Hawaii law defines marijuana as “any part of the plant (genus) cannabis.” HRS 712-1240. Shown: a pressed Cannabis sativa specimen.
Possession of three grams or less is a civil violation with a $130 fine. Possession of more than three grams is a petty misdemeanor under HRS 712-1249.
Federal law now treats marijuana under a state medical license as Schedule III. The federal order took effect April 28, 2026. Other marijuana remains Schedule I. Current as of November 12, 2026.

glossary.definition: Moving to Schedule III would place cannabis alongside drugs like testosterone and Tylenol with codeine, substances the government recognizes as medically useful but still regulates.
Processing delays meant patients often waited days to receive their 329 cards, the state-issued identification required for dispensary purchases.

onScreen: December, Seeds and the Home Grower What the federal hemp change says about seeds.
Two dates, not one. November 12, 2026 starts the first exclusion. December 11, 2026 starts the rest. Until then the 2018 wording applies, unless Congress acts again.
2018: seeds counted as hemp. Hemp includes “the seeds thereof” at 0.3 percent delta-9 THC, dry weight. The text does not say whose THC counts for a seed.
The new test looks at the plant. Viable seeds from a plant over 0.3 percent total THC, counting THCA, are not hemp. Pub. L. 119-37, section 781.
Industrial hemp seed stays hemp. Seed grown for grain, oil, cake, nut or hull, for microgreens, or made only for those uses is inside the industrial hemp definition.
Excluded products fall back under the CSA. The Congressional Research Service says they “would instead be subject to regulation under the CSA as marijuana.”
Shipping protections name hemp. Section 10114 and section 737 cover hemp grown under farm bill programs. They do not address seeds excluded from hemp.
Hawaii already bars selling viable hemp seeds. Rule 11-37-3 allows sales only to a USDA-licensed hemp producer or a permitted hemp processor. DOH lists all viable hemp seeds as prohibited.
State law counts seeds as marijuana. HRS 712-1240 defines marijuana to include the seeds. Its hemp exceptions turn on who holds the hemp or on a finished product.
Hawaii's hemp chapter has an end date. The code's notes repeal chapter 328G on July 1, 2027, unless the legislature acts.
The patient statute does not name seeds. OMCCR lists three sources: a licensed dispensary, personal growing, a registered caregiver. Its guidance does not mention seeds.

onScreen: When US law banned ceremony. In 1883 an Interior Department rule made the sun dance an "Indian offense," punished by the loss of rations.
It began with a letter. In December 1882 Interior Secretary Henry M. Teller asked for rules to "restrict and ultimately abolish" the dances and the work of medicine men.
A jail term with no fixed end. Rule 6 jailed a medicine man for at least ten days, or until he promised, "approved by the agent," to "forever abandon" his practices.
1888: a judge upheld the court. No act of Congress created it. Judge Matthew Deady called the courts "mere educational and disciplinary instrumentalities."
1904: "so-called religious ceremonies." The rewritten rules named the sun dance "and all other similar dances and so-called religious ceremonies" as "Indian offenses."
1978: Congress set a policy. It admitted ceremonies had been "in a few instances banned." In 1988 the Supreme Court found the act gave no right to sue.
The court still sits. In 2022 the Supreme Court counted five CFR courts serving 16 tribes. Their code today has no religious offenses.

onScreen: Hawaii's Cannabis Market What the State's Own Data Reveals
Hawaii's medical cannabis dispensaries capture 86 to 87% of every dollar their patients spend on cannabis. Source: a December 2025 analysis written for the Hawaii Department of Health.
Hawaii's legal medical cannabis market brings in about $5.3 million a month, or about $64 million a year. That is about 33% of the whole market, gray and illicit sources included.
For March, BioTrack logged $5,336,706 in medical cannabis sales. The survey estimated $5,409,537, a 98.6% match.
Patients on Molokai and Lanai report trips of nearly 70 and 90 minutes to the nearest dispensary. Few answers came from those islands. The state lists no dispensary on either one.
In a survey in Japan, 57.5% said legal adult use would have no influence on a decision to visit Hawaii. 1,009 answers, October 2025. It measures what people say, not trips taken.
The report's projection for year five of legal adult use. All sources, per month, year five. Adjusted for a 15% tax: $46 to $90 million; Not adjusted: $59 to $95 million.
The report does not estimate tax revenue. It says any external application of a flat tax rate to its projections should be interpreted with caution.
With legal adult use, Hawaii would need about 117,500 plants harvested and cured a year, the report estimates. It scales up medical growers' BioTrack data from 2019 to 2024.
In 2026, HB 1624 proposed a constitutional amendment to legalize adult use. In February, House Speaker Nadine Nakamura said neither it nor HB 1625 would move ahead.

1900: section 98 named five ships. It gave them American registers and put trade between the islands and the rest of the country under the coasting laws.
1920: the Jones Act. Senator Wesley Jones changed the cargo rule in section 27 so it covered goods moving by land and water between American points.
Almost everything comes by sea. More than 90 percent of the goods imported into Hawaiʻi enter through Honolulu Harbor, the state says.
American-built ships cost more. A U.S.-built ship cost 1.2 times a foreign one in 1922. By 2019 a tanker was about four times the world price.

posts.title: When Two Versions of the Law Disagree
posts.summary: For nearly a century the Hawaiian Kingdom and then the Territory published their laws twice, once in Hawaiian and once in English. When the two texts said different things, someone had to decide which one was the law. The answer changed in 1859, and the Legislature is still arguing about it.

slides.alt: A black-and-white photograph from about 1870 of Aliʻiōlani Hale in Honolulu, a two-story stone government building with a clock tower and a tall flagpole in an open yard. It was the Kingdom government building that later housed its Legislature and Supreme Court.
slides.credit: Photo: HABS / Hawaii State Archives, PD
slides.url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:GENERAL_EXTERIOR_VIEW_OF_NORTHEAST_(FRONT)_ELEVATION_FROM_EAST_(Photo_ca_1870,_from_original_in_Hawaii_State_Arvhices).__Photocopy_1966_-_Aliiolani_Hale,_463_King_Street,_Honolulu,_HABS_HI,2-HONLU,3-21.tif (HABS HI-2-HONLU-3-21, 1966 photocopy of a c. 1870 print in the Hawaii State Archives; cropped to the print)

slides.alt: Page 6 of the Compiler's Preface to the 1846 Statute Laws, in old printed type. It says the code went to the king's cabinet for discussion, then to the Rev. William Richards for faithful translation into the native language, then to both houses for three readings, debated section by section.

Page 259 of volume 1 of the Hawaiian Reports, headed 1856, Hardy vs. Ruggles, in old printed type. The lines read that where there is a radical and irreconcilable difference between the English and Hawaiian, the latter must govern, because it is the language of the legislators of the country.

Page 367 of the 1859 Civil Code, Chapter XLI, General Provisions, in old printed type. Section 1493 says that if a radical and irreconcilable difference is found between the English and Hawaiian versions of any part of the Code, the English version shall be held binding. The page ends with the approval of May 17, 1859, signed Kamehameha.

Four lines of old printed type from the same page of Hardy v. Ruggles. They read that the English and Hawaiian may often be used to help and explain each other where the meaning is obscure, or the contradiction slight, but where the omission in the Hawaiian is clear, it is impossible to reconcile them.

A printed act headed An Act for the Construction of Statutes Where the English and Hawaiian Versions Do Not Agree. Its one section says that whenever a radical and irreconcilable difference is found between the English and Hawaiian version of any of the laws of the Kingdom, which have been, or may hereafter be enacted, the English version shall be held binding. Approved January 10, 1865, signed Kamehameha R.
slides.credit: Source: Laws of 1864 to 1865, p. 68, PD

slides.alt: A 1943 session-law page headed Promulgation of Laws. Act 218 rewrites the rule so that the secretary of the Territory publishes the laws once in the English language in a Honolulu daily newspaper. The Hawaiian-language publication is gone from the text.

Two crops of a 1979 session-law page, Act 97, S.B. No. 45. It rewrites section 1-13: English and Hawaiian are the official languages of Hawaii; where there is a radical and irreconcilable difference between the English and Hawaiian version of any state law, the English version shall be held binding; Hawaiian shall not be required for public acts and transactions.

A typed bill page, S.B. No. 16, H.D. 1, with numbered lines. Underlined new text adds a proviso to section 1-13: if a law was originally drafted in Hawaiian and its English version was translated from it, and the law has not been subsequently amended, codified, recodified or reenacted in English, the Hawaiian version shall be held binding.

A typed bill page, S.B. No. 109, S.D. 2, H.D. 1, with numbered lines. Underlined text adds the same proviso for laws originally drafted in Hawaiian and not later amended, codified, recodified or reenacted in English. Its last line reads: This Act shall take effect on July 1, 3000.

A typed bill page, H.B. No. 2433, H.D. 1, S.D. 1, with numbered lines. The sentence making the English version binding is struck through. New underlined text gives priority to the language that aligns with the intent of the legislature as evidenced by legislative history, context and purpose. The last line sets the effective date at March 22, 2075.

Seven lines of old printed type from page 480 of volume 8 of the Hawaiian Reports, April 1892, In re Ross. They read that the English version shall be held binding, that the two versions constitute but one act, that there is no dual legislation, and that as a rule one version is the translation of the other.

The top of page 69 of volume 2 of the Hawaiian Reports, 1858, Levi Haalelea v. Daniel Montgomery, in old printed type. It reads that the deed is a printed formula in two languages, that the English version of this formula is, of course, the original, and the Hawaiian merely a translation.

onScreen: When Two Versions of the Law Disagree The Hawaiian Kingdom governed through laws published in Hawaiian and English.

A law was drafted in one language and translated into the other. In 1845 and 1846, Attorney General John Ricord drafted the new laws in English. William Richards translated them into Hawaiian, and both houses gave each act three readings.

In Hardy v. Ruggles (1856), the Hawaiian Kingdom’s Supreme Court held that where the English and Hawaiian versions differ in a radical and irreconcilable way, the Hawaiian governs, “because it is the language of the legislators of the country.”
The 1859 Civil Code decided it the other way three years later.
Where wording was obscure or the contradiction slight, the Hawaiian and English could be used to help explain one another.
In 1865 the English rule was extended to every law of the Kingdom, both those already passed and those passed later.
From 1943 the Territory published its new laws in English only. When only one language is routinely produced, later researchers do not encounter two parallel witnesses.
HRS section 1-13 today:
A 2023 bill proposed Hawaiian priority when a law was originally drafted in Hawaiian. A House committee limited it to laws not later amended, codified or reenacted in English. It did not become law.
Senate Bill 109 carried the same approach into the 2025 to 2026 session, but it did not become law. A House draft set its effective date at July 1, 3000.
A 2026 draft looked to intent instead. House Bill 2433 would give priority to the version that matches the Legislature’s intent. The Senate draft’s effective date is March 22, 2075.
What We Actually Know
The durable technological lesson is narrower and stronger.

posts.title: The Observatory That Turned a Volcano into a Century-Long Signal
posts.summary: Part 1 of 2. In 1912 a geologist began measuring Kīlauea every day and writing the numbers down. This part follows the logbooks, cellars, gas tubes and warnings of the observatory's first decades. It also follows the people who kept the measurements going when the founder was away.

onScreen: The year Hawaii rewrote the 329 card Acts 46, 241 and 269 of 2025: certification, telehealth, fees, caregivers and hemp sellers.
Three laws in 2025 Act 46 was approved May 14. Act 241 followed on June 27, and Act 269 on July 2.
A new way to qualify A primary treating medical provider can certify a condition not on the debilitating list. A hospice provider can certify hospice care.
Who counts as a primary treating provider A Hawaii physician or APRN, licensed in the state, primarily responsible for your treatment and ongoing care.
Telehealth is allowed No initial in-person visit is required. The provider must be in Hawaii and meet the same standard of care. OMCCR's guidance starts September 18, 2025.
A cap on certification fees No more than three times the Department's registration fee. OMCCR's fee page caps it at $105 for one year and $315 for three.
The Department can inspect files It may inspect the files behind a certification, and suspend or revoke a provider who refuses.
Caregivers can grow again Act 46 restored caregiver cultivation, retroactive to January 1, 2025. Fines can reach $5,000 per violation, and each day counts separately.
Five patients A caregiver may serve up to five patients. Each growing location may be used for not more than five patients.
A cultivator license starts in 2028 From January 1, 2028, Act 241 Part IV makes it unlawful for any person to cultivate cannabis without a Department license.
Hemp sellers must register Since January 1, 2026, hemp product retailers and distributors need a certificate: $50, valid five years. Topicals and tinctures are exempt.
What we know and what we do not
Education, not legal advice OMCCR's own guidance sheets say they do not replace legal advice, and neither does this. For your situation, ask a Hawaiʻi attorney.

posts.title: The Gate That Thinks With the Tide
posts.summary: Heʻeia Fishpond is enclosed by a stone wall about 1.3 miles long, and its gates admit water and small fish while keeping grown fish home. Floods, mangrove, a fish die-off and a stream diversion broke that system. The studies and reports on its rebuilding show what the gates do, and what they still lack.

onScreen: The Gate That Thinks With the Tide The kuapā curves through Kāneʻohe Bay, built from stone and coral without becoming an impermeable barrier.
Inside, those flows make a brackish environment where limu and other food for fish can grow.
A mākāhā is often translated as a sluice gate.
The openings permit water and small fish to move. Juvenile fish can enter.
No reliable source identifies one person who designed Heʻeia Fishpond. Its wall is therefore not only a structure.
It is evidence of coordination: people selecting and moving material, reading a difficult coastal environment, organizing labor, maintaining a shared food system, and transferring knowledge.
The labor did not end when the wall was completed. Its productive capacity depends on continuous mālama: clearing channels, repairing storm damage, maintaining gates, observing fish and water,
controlling predators or invasive species, coordinating harvests, and caring for relationships upstream and downstream. Loko iʻa are living systems.

The physical system at Heʻeia makes that labor legible. Paepae o Heʻeia describes a wall built in compact layers that slow water loss, preserve a base level at low tide, and concentrate more exchange through seven mākāhā.
Together they help maintain brackish conditions favorable to limu and fish.

Restoration practitioners face watersheds altered by development, sediment and nutrient changes, invasive species, unreliable recruitment of juvenile fish, warmer water, storms, regulation, funding constraints, and the sheer physical demand of maintaining a coastal structure.

posts.title: The Lines That Changed the Land
posts.summary: Between 1846 and 1855, Hawaiʻi asked thousands of people to turn the land they lived on into written claims, testimony, surveys and awards. The laws, the award books and the surveyors' own accounts show how the lines were drawn, who drew them, and why courts still read them today.

It is an actual parcel made legible as a drawing, a description and a signed document, which is the sentence this story opens with.

onScreen: The Lines That Changed the Land Before land can be sold as a parcel, it must be made legible as one.

A boundary must be described in words, followed across the ground, measured, calculated, drawn, attached to a name or number, accepted by an institution, and preserved in a document another institution will recognize.
A claimant did not present land itself to the commission.
A boundary known through a stream, a wall, a planting area, a ridge, a neighboring holding, or the memory of people in a place could be restated as a sequence of courses and distances.
The description could be calculated, copied, mapped, indexed, compared, and carried into a later dispute.
The lines on a cadastral map therefore deserve to be read twice. First as measurements: carefully made descriptions that allowed a boundary to be found again.

Second as instruments: documents that could transfer, divide, mortgage, foreclose, and settle a claim without anyone returning to the ground the boundary describes. Educational information, not legal advice.

The First Amendment has been read to protect the content of belief. Substantive due process has been held to protect intimate decisions about body, family, and identity.

Stanley v. Georgia (1969) "If the First Amendment means anything, it means that a State has no business telling a man, sitting alone in his own house, what books he may read or what films he may watch."
The Glucksberg test has two parts. The interest must be "deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition," and the Court requires a "careful description" of it.
Dobbs may be the most serious structural challenge. Dobbs (2022) overruled Roe and Casey. The article says cognitive liberty has not been recognized as a constitutional right in prior doctrine.
Smith: neutral, generally applicable laws Employment Division v. Smith held that the Free Exercise Clause does not require religious exemptions from neutral, generally applicable laws.
Raich and the commerce power Raich is a significant obstacle to any facial challenge to the CSA on Commerce Clause grounds.
What we know: Psilocybin and psilocyn, compounds in mushrooms like this liberty cap, remain in Schedule I as of November 15, 2026 (21 CFR 1308.11(d)).
What we don't know: The article reports that no federal court has ruled on a cognitive liberty claim. It says a court's answer cannot be predicted.
Describe the interest before you argue for it. What exactly is the interest being claimed? Is there a history and tradition behind that exact interest? Does the science show it, or only suggest it?

posts.title: Who donates a brain, and who decides?
posts.summary: The law says a signed gift belongs to the person who signed it. The national brain bank network still asks the family to sign at the time of death. onScreen: Who donates a brain, and who decides? Illinois law says that once a donor signs, a person other than the donor "is barred from changing, amending, or revoking" the gift.
The brain banks still ask the family. The NIH brain bank network tells donors that "a consent form must be signed by the next of kin at the time of death."
A license sticker is not enough. The network's own answer: the sticker on a driver's license "does not give brain banks permission to receive a brain."
No signature? A ladder decides. Illinois lists 11 classes, from a health care agent and a spouse down to a close friend. No one lower may decide if someone higher can be reached.
Signed is not the same as done. At Rush in Chicago, most signers in two studies came to autopsy. Among African American signers, 53.4 percent did, as of 2012.
A coroner can keep the brain. In 2008 Ohio's top court held that families had no protected right in organs a coroner removed and kept for testing.
Sometimes it is one phone call. Asked by phone on the day of an autopsy, 69.7 percent of families said yes: 74.1 percent of White families and 57.0 percent of Black families.

posts.title: The Machine Inside the Mountain
posts.summary: Part 1 of 2. In 1913 a sugar company drove a tunnel under the Koʻolau Range to carry stream water across Oʻahu. The mountain answered with more water than anyone had measured. This part follows the building of the ditch and what it took from the streams.

slides.alt: Black-and-white 1916 photograph looking down a timbered tunnel in the Waiāhole project: curved wooden arch forms overhead, a plank wall on the right and narrow rail tracks on the floor leading into the dark. The report's own caption reads 'Portion of tunnel, showing forms for arch of tunnel roof' and does not say which tunnel or heading. It opens the story inside the mountain, on the machine itself.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: USGS map of the Waiāhole Ditch System: a blue dotted line starts at the Kahana tunnels in the windward valleys, runs south past Waikāne and Uwao tunnels and Gates 30 and 31, passes under the Koʻolau at the North Portal, comes out past Adit 8 and crosses central Oʻahu to Reservoir 155. Black outlines mark the Kahana, Waikāne and Waiāhole watersheds the ditch draws from.

Black-and-white 1916 photograph of two large riveted steel pipes arching over a cut in a hillside at Waikakalaua Gulch, with a railway track running through the cut below. The report's caption calls them steel pipes crossing a branch of the Oahu Railway, the larger one the new 72-inch pipe. They are the part of the route where the conduit crosses a gulch instead of a tunnel or ditch.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: First page of Act 111, Session Laws of Hawaiʻi 1998, the law that let the state buy the Waiāhole water system. Section 2 opens: Water belongs to the people and the State should be the steward in managing and ensuring the allocation of this resource for the highest and best use in the public interest.

Black-and-white 1916 photograph of a worker in a hat standing before two concrete-framed gates with hand wheels above them, set into the mouth of a finished section of the conduit. The report captions it 'Gates at a section of finished conduit.' It shows the kind of gate the sentence means, the control that moves in minutes.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: Printed paragraph from page 111 of the 2000 Waiāhole opinion: For the reasons fully explained below, we affirm in part and vacate in part the Commission's decision and remand for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

The caption of the opinion as printed on page 97 of the Hawaiʻi Reports: In the Matter of the Water Use Permit Applications ... for the Waiāhole Ditch Combined Contested Case Hearing. No. 21309. Supreme Court of Hawaiʻi. Aug. 22, 2000.

Letterhead of the State of Hawaiʻi Commission on Water Resource Management, dated December 24, 1997. The letter tells the parties that the Commission's Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law and Decision and Order for the Waiāhole Ditch Combined Contested Case Hearing are enclosed: the decision the Supreme Court later reviewed.

Black-and-white 2019 photograph of two large siphon pipes crossing Kipapa Gulch side by side: on the left a newer siphon behind a concrete intake with a wooden screen, on the right the historic riveted-steel siphon behind a rusted grate. The survey caption says the historic one is no longer in use and the newer one is in use. It shows the fixed physical network of the Waiāhole Ditch carrying today's water through 1916-era works.

Lines of type from page 6 of Kluegel's 1916 report: the highest intake at 790 feet, and the length of the main tunnel through the Koolau Ridge, 14,567 feet, or 2.76 miles, with the North Portal at 752 feet and the South Portal at 724 feet. The usual facts, which the slide says are not the only questions.

Black-and-white 1916 photograph inside the main tunnel: a wall of dark rock with water jetting and spraying out of it into the bore, and two men with lanterns standing near the floor. The report's caption reads 'Water issuing from water-bearing rock in the main tunnel, 10,550 feet from the South Portal, March 23, 1915,' and explains that the lanterns are held by men beside a drill. It shows the mountain's own stored groundwater, the landscape process the tunnel tapped.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: Black-and-white 1914 photograph of six tunnel workers in work clothes and caps standing together underground in front of a rock face, with a drill rig and air hose across the foreground. The report's caption reads 'Japanese professional tunnel men, Main Tunnel, July, 1914,' and its text credits them with most of the drilling and mucking. It puts the people who built the tunnel in the frame.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: Paragraph from page 178 of a 1913 USGS report, written about 1911, before the ditch: Waiāhole Stream rises in springs about 1,000 feet above sea level, its flow is fairly constant, and a part of the water is used for irrigating rice and taro lands in the lower part of the valley.

Typed lines from page 3 of a 2025 Hawaiʻi Senate bill on the Waiāhole water system, listing who depends on it today: Aloun Farms, the Hawaii Agriculture Research Center, Larry Jefts Farm, Mililani Nursery, Mililani Agricultural Park, Sugarland Farms, Waiawa Nursery, Waikele Farms, livestock ranchers, Mililani Memorial Park and the Waiawa correctional facility.

A Parshall flume on the Waiāhole Ditch near Mililani in June 2019 (HAER HI-146-8): a concrete channel that narrows in the middle so one depth reading gives a flow rate, with smooth fast water and tall grass on the banks. By 2019 a laser sensor upstream had replaced it. It shows a gauge, the subject of the line.

Page 728 of a 1921 territorial Supreme Court opinion setting out the deals made before the tunnel was dug: a fifty-year lease of Kahana's surplus water from May 27, 1916, and a December 30, 1912 deed of water rights in Kahana, Waikāne and Waiāhole for $257,500, each subject to the valley residents' water for household use and irrigation.

The start of the conclusion of the 2000 Waiāhole opinion, page 189: For the reasons stated in this opinion, we vacate in part the Commission's decision and remand for additional findings and conclusions ... regarding the following, beginning with an interim instream flow standard for windward streams.

Faded photograph from a 1913 USGS paper, captioned Velocity-area gaging station, Waiāhole Stream: two men measure the stream by wading it, one seated in the water and one holding a rod, while men in hats watch from the grassy bank. A flow measurement, the thing the line says cannot decide allocation on its own.

A metal gate set into the concrete wall of the Waiāhole Ditch near Mililani, with a staff scale marked in one-foot steps and a narrow concrete footbridge at right, photographed for the National Park Service HAER survey in June 2019 (HAER HI-146-4). The 1916 machine still decides, gate by gate, where today's water goes.
slides.credit: Photo: David Franzen, HAER, Public domain

slides.alt: Line chart from the USGS low-flow study, Figure 34: daily water released at Gate 31 to Waiāhole Stream from January 1999 to late 2004, a jagged blue line mostly between 5 and 25 million gallons a day, above a flat pink line for the Commission's targeted restoration flow of 4, then 4.8 million gallons a day.

onScreen: The Machine Inside the Mountain Inside Oʻahu’s Koʻolau Mountains, the Waiāhole tunnel still helps decide where water goes.
The project therefore did not simply capture rainfall after it entered a ditch. It recruited an entire mountain watershed.
Intakes, tunnels, ditches, siphons, reservoirs, and gates turned flow into a controllable route.
Once farms, towns, ecosystems, and institutions depend on a route, infrastructure becomes governance.
A gate can change flow in minutes. Deciding the lawful and sustainable flow can take years.
In 2000, the Hawaiʻi Supreme Court affirmed part of the Commission on Water Resource Management’s decision, vacated part and sent issues back.
Waiāhole’s present consequence is therefore a continuing design problem: how should a fixed physical network serve changing public purposes?
Ask which landscape processes it recruited,
whose labor made it durable,
what uses it displaced,
which dependencies formed around it,
what the gauges can and cannot tell us,
and which past decision is hiding inside the present baseline.

Who can certify Physicians and APRNs can certify when they have a bona fide relationship with you. Hospice providers can certify hospice patients.
OMCCR lists but does not vouch The list is not exhaustive. The Department of Health does not endorse providers or guarantee the list, and encourages patients to research them.
Ask about cannabis education OMCCR’s patient page says meeting a provider who has completed medical cannabis education is advisable. Its specialist list was under development on October 11, 2026.
The first visit can be telehealth Act 241 says the relationship need not start with an in-person visit. OMCCR says telehealth certification has been allowed since September 18, 2025.
Telehealth has rules The provider must be physically in Hawaiʻi during the visit. Telehealth must meet the same standard of care as an in-person visit.
A form alone is not enough OMCCR says an online questionnaire alone does not meet the standard of care. Each patient must be assessed individually.
What a visit may include Providers told OMCCR what to expect: bring ID, medical files and your medication list; expect a history review and a check for drug interactions.
The fee has a cap A certifier’s fee may not exceed three times the state registration fee, $105 for a 1-year certification. Fees must be disclosed first.
Rules moved after September 2024 That month’s newsletter said telehealth was for renewals only. Act 241 and OMCCR’s September 2025 guidance now allow telehealth for first visits.

posts.title: Embed, host or repost? Big Buck Bunny on YouTube
posts.summary: A rabbit cartoon from Amsterdam was made to be shared, and its makers put it on YouTube themselves. That makes it a clean test case. Showing YouTube's player on a web page, holding the file and uploading a fresh copy look alike to a viewer. The license, YouTube's terms and the courts treat them as three separate acts.

slides.alt: A frame from Big Buck Bunny, taken at 1:15 from the Blender Foundation's own 1080p release file: the large gray cartoon rabbit smiles behind white flowers in a meadow. It is the free, Creative Commons licensed film the sentence names.

Page 8 of the Ninth Circuit's 2023 opinion in Hunley v. Instagram, cropped to the paragraph that ends: Importantly, the embedding website does not store a copy of the underlying image. It is the court's own statement that an embed is not a new copy.

The entrance of the Studio/K cinema in Amsterdam on April 10, 2008, the premiere night of Big Buck Bunny: a red carpet between chrome posts and red ropes, a tall white rabbit cutout by the doors and bicycles parked to the right. It is the launch of the 2008 release the sentence describes.
slides.credit: Photo: William Maanders, CC BY 3.0 NL

slides.alt: The license card from the film's closing credits, at 9:39: white capital letters on a streaked brown background read Licensed as Creative Commons Attribute 3.0, and below it, www.bigbuckbunny.org. It is the license notice the film itself carries.

Section 3, License Grant, of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 legal code: a worldwide, royalty-free, non-exclusive, perpetual license to reproduce the work and include it in collections. It is the clause that permits the broad reuse the sentence names.

The start of section 4(b) of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 legal code, the credit clause: anyone who distributes or performs the work must keep intact all copyright notices and give credit reasonable to the medium, beginning with the name of the original author. It is the attribution condition the sentence says must be followed.

The entrance of YouTube's headquarters at 901 Cherry Avenue in San Bruno, California, with a YouTube sign on a hedge-covered wall, photographed August 9, 2010. It is the company that hosts uploaded copies on its own servers, the host the sentence names. It does not show where any file is stored.

Page 9 of the Ninth Circuit's opinion in Hunley v. Instagram: the host server can control whether embedding is available and can delete or replace the image, and the browser shows whatever the host server supplies. It is the court's account of an embed showing the host's own copy on another page.

Page 34 of the Ninth Circuit's opinion in Hunley v. Instagram, cropped to the passage that says BuzzFeed and Time embedded but did not store the underlying photographs, so they did not directly infringe. It is the court applying the point that an embed makes no new copy of the file.

A chart titled Each upload is a new file, with three boxes: the YouTube upload of May 29, 2008 (9:57, license in the description only), the 4K YouTube upload of Nov 10, 2014 (YouTube's CC BY label), and the same 4K version on Blender's PeerTube site, Oct 27, 2018 (license field Attribution). It shows one film as several separate uploaded files, as the sentence says a repost is.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from YouTube data

slides.alt: Paragraph 44 of the EU Court of Justice's 2018 Renckhoff judgment: posting a work on another website gives rise to a new communication, independent of the one first authorized, which may stay available after the author removes the original. It is the court's statement that a repost is a separate copy needing its own permission.

Section 4(a) of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 legal code: you must include a copy of, or the web address for, this License with every copy of the work you distribute or perform. It is the license link the sentence says to keep with the file.

Section 3(b) of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 legal code: an adaptation must clearly label that changes were made, for example with the line The original work has been modified. It is the modification note the sentence asks for. Captions and transcripts are not license terms and are not shown.

A chart titled Host, embed or repost, with three boxes. Host: the file is on YouTube's servers, allowed by the uploader's license to YouTube. Embed: the file stays on YouTube and the page holds code that calls the player, allowed by YouTube's Terms. Repost: a separate copy that may outlast the original, allowed for this film by CC BY 3.0 and its conditions. It lays out the route choice the sentence asks for.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from source data

slides.alt: Page 36 of the Second Circuit's April 2026 opinion in Richardson v. Townsquare Media, quoting the License to Other Users clause of YouTube's terms, which covers use only as enabled by a feature of the service, such as video playback or embeds. It is the permission that comes with the embed route.

Section 106 of Title 17 of the United States Code, Exclusive rights in copyrighted works, from the 2023 edition printed by the Government Publishing Office, cropped to the heading and the first three rights: to reproduce, to prepare derivative works and to distribute copies. These are the owner's rights that still apply when a file is not openly licensed.

posts.title: The per-container cap: how the new hemp law measures a package
posts.summary: The 2025 hemp law caps finished products at 0.4 milligrams of THC per container. Here is the text, the definition of a container, the federal data on children that framed the debate, and what is still undecided.

slides.alt: Young hemp plants, Cannabis sativa, growing thickly in raised beds inside a plastic-covered high tunnel in Crawford County, Indiana, with a water tank behind; no people in frame. Slide text: The new hemp cap counts the package. Hemp in an Indiana high tunnel, June 2022. A 2025 law caps the THC in each package of finished products made from it.
slides.credit: Photo: B. O'Connor, USDA NRCS, PD

slides.alt: A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 559: clause (iv), excluding final hemp-derived cannabinoid products with greater than 0.4 milligrams combined total per container of total THC and similar-effect cannabinoids. Slide text: 0.4 milligrams per container. A final product is not hemp if its container holds over 0.4 mg combined of total THC and THC look-alikes, as HHS decides.

A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 560: the definition of container as the innermost wrapping, packaging or vessel in direct contact with the product, and the exclusion of bulk shipping containers. Slide text: The container is the innermost pack. The law names "a jar, bottle, bag, box, packet, can, carton, or cartridge." Bulk shipping boxes and outer wraps do not count.

A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 559: intermediate products excluded above 0.3 percent combined total, and when marketed or sold as a final product or directly to an end consumer. Slide text: Ingredients get a different line. Intermediate products are limited to 0.3 percent combined, and may not be marketed or sold to an end consumer at all.

A crop of an FDA web page: national poison control centers received 2,362 exposure cases of delta-8 THC products from January 1, 2021 to February 28, 2022; 41 percent involved patients under 18; 82 percent of unintentional exposures affected children. Slide text: FDA's 2022 count: 41 percent were under 18. Poison centers took 2,362 delta-8 THC cases in 14 months. 41 percent involved people under 18. FDA notes these are self-reported calls.

A crop of an FDA web page, point 5: delta-8 THC products should be kept out of the reach of children and pets, with a paragraph on packaging such as gummies and candies and sales at convenience stores and gas stations. Slide text: FDA's concern was the package. FDA warned of packaging "that may appeal to children" and sales where there may be no age limit. Its advice: keep products out of reach.

A crop of the Federal Register, December 23, 2025: Executive Order 14370 saying some full-spectrum CBD products will once again be controlled as marijuana when section 781 goes into effect because of the per-container threshold. Slide text: Full-spectrum CBD is caught too. A December 2025 executive order says some full-spectrum CBD products will be controlled as marijuana once the per-container cap applies.

A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 561: item (D), additional information and specificity about the term container. Slide text: Still open: what counts as a container. FDA was told to give more detail on "container" within 90 days. As of Nov. 12, 2026, nothing was in the Federal Register.

onScreen: The new hemp cap counts the package. Hemp in an Indiana high tunnel, June 2022. A 2025 law caps the THC in each package of finished products made from it.
0.4 milligrams per container. A final product is not hemp if its container holds over 0.4 mg combined of total THC and THC look-alikes, as HHS decides.
The container is the innermost pack. The law names "a jar, bottle, bag, box, packet, can, carton, or cartridge." Bulk shipping boxes and outer wraps do not count.
Ingredients get a different line. Intermediate products are limited to 0.3 percent combined, and may not be marketed or sold to an end consumer at all.
FDA's 2022 count: 41 percent were under 18. Poison centers took 2,362 delta-8 THC cases in 14 months. 41 percent involved people under 18. FDA notes these are self-reported calls.
FDA's concern was the package. FDA warned of packaging "that may appeal to children" and sales where there may be no age limit. Its advice: keep products out of reach.
Full-spectrum CBD is caught too. A December 2025 executive order says some full-spectrum CBD products will be controlled as marijuana once the per-container cap applies.
Still open: what counts as a container. FDA was told to give more detail on "container" within 90 days. As of Nov. 12, 2026, nothing was in the Federal Register.

glossary.definition: "Per container" means the limit is for the whole package, not a serving or a gram.

'container' means the innermost wrapping, packaging, or vessel in direct contact with a final hemp-derived cannabinoid product in which the final hemp-derived cannabinoid product is enclosed for retail sale to consumers

A hemp-derived cannabinoid product is any product from hemp, other than industrial hemp, that "contains cannabinoids in any form" and "is intended for human or animal use through any means of application or administration, such as inhalation, ingestion, or topical application"
